patients.summary: Graduate student with bipolar I disorder on lithium who joined in 2021, developed lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus diagnosed at his last practice visit in January 2025, and in July 2026 was hospitalized for valproate-induced liver injury with hyperammonemia two weeks after divalproex was added at a psychiatric admission. The practice learns of the 2026 events from his message and late records and has not seen him since.

documents.title: New Patient Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
23 y/o man, second-year graduate student, here to set up primary care. Had been using student health and wants a doctor who will stay put.

PMH: Bipolar I disorder, diagnosed 2016 in his first year of college. Followed since by an outside psychiatrist, seen every 3 months or so. On lithium the whole time; no episodes he'd call significant in several years. Psychiatry checks levels, but he is fine with us drawing them with his yearly labs and sending copies over.
PSH: tonsils out at 8.
Meds: lithium carbonate 300 mg caps, 2 caps twice a day (600 mg BID). Rx from psychiatry.
Allergies: none known.
FHx: mother has bipolar disorder and a thyroid problem he thinks is autoimmune, on thyroid pills. Father has high blood pressure. No sibs mentioned.
Social: lives with one roommate near campus. Never smoked. Doesn't drink at all, partly because of the lithium. No drug use. Bikes most places.
Vaccines: Tdap 2019 at student health; Pfizer x2 in April.

ROS: sleeping 7-8 h, mood even, appetite normal. No tremor he notices. No unusual thirst or urination. Nothing else.

Exam: well, relaxed, good eye contact. Vitals as recorded, BMI about 24. HEENT clear, tonsillar fossae empty. Thyroid not enlarged, no nodules. Heart RRR without murmur. Lungs clear. Abdomen soft, no organomegaly. No tremor with arms outstretched. Skin without rash. Neuro grossly normal.
PHQ-9: 3.

A/P
1. Bipolar I disorder, stable on lithium with outside psychiatry. Baseline CMP, CBC, TSH and lithium level today; results to go to his psychiatrist as well. Records requested.
2. Health maintenance: one-time HCV and HIV screens today, lipids since he has never had them. Flu shot when this season's vaccine arrives.
RTC one year for a physical, sooner as needed.

documents.title: Your lab results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Gavin, everything from Wednesday came back normal. Kidney numbers, sodium, calcium, liver tests, blood counts and thyroid are all in range. Lithium level 0.7, which sits in the usual target window. Cholesterol is fine, and the hepatitis C and HIV screens are negative. I'm faxing a copy to your psychiatrist's office. Nice to meet you.

documents.title: Records from university student health service
documents.author: student health
documents.body:
Received 9/8/2021, 22 pages. University student health service, visits 2016 to 2021.

Summary on review: routine visits only. Tdap given 08/21/2019. COVID-19 Pfizer doses 04/07/2021 and 04/28/2021. Bipolar disorder noted on every problem list with lithium, managed by outside psychiatry. Labs over those years limited to occasional BMP and TSH copied from psychiatry, all normal. Allergies listed as none. No surgeries besides childhood tonsillectomy.

Scanned. Immunizations reconciled. -- MA

documents.author: RN
documents.body: Came in after his afternoon lab section for flu vaccine. Screening questions negative, no egg or vaccine reactions, feels well. Quadrivalent flu 0.5 mL IM L deltoid. VIS given. Waited 15 min in the lobby, no reaction, left on his bike.

documents.title: Outpatient psychiatry summary
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
Outpatient Psychiatry - Treatment Summary
In response to records request dated 08/04/2021

Mr. Michaud has been in our care since 2016, when bipolar I disorder was diagnosed during his first year of college. He has been maintained on lithium carbonate since diagnosis, currently 600 mg twice daily, with serum levels between 0.6 and 0.8 mmol/L. He has been euthymic for several years without psychiatric admission in that time. Insight and adherence are good. He tolerates lithium without notable tremor or GI effects.

We see him roughly quarterly and will continue to prescribe. Thank you for sharing his August labs; we would appreciate copies of future renal, thyroid and lithium results.

Allergies: NKDA.
Medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg capsules, two capsules by mouth twice daily.

Outpatient psychiatry, attending psychiatrist

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Yearly visit. Spent the summer on field work, back to classes and teaching a section this term. Psychiatry visits continue every few months; no dose changes, mood steady, sleep fine.

Meds: lithium 600 mg BID (psychiatry). NKDA.
ROS negative, including no tremor, no change in thirst or urination, no weight change.

Exam: vitals as charted, weight stable. Thyroid normal size. Heart and lungs normal. Abdomen soft. Hands steady. Skin fine.
PHQ-9 2.

A/P
- Bipolar I, stable on lithium. BMP, CBC, TSH, lithium level today, copy to psychiatry.
- Flu and the new bivalent COVID booster today, one in each arm.
- Screening otherwise current for age. See him in a year.

documents.title: Lab results from your physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gavin - all normal again. Sodium, kidney function and calcium in range, thyroid normal, blood counts fine. Lithium 0.8. Copy sent to your psychiatrist. Talk next year unless something comes up.

documents.title: Annual Physical
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Rescheduled from last month. Now in his fourth year, working toward his qualifying exam this winter, so more hours at the desk and less sleep some weeks, but says mood is even and his psychiatrist agrees. Still lithium 600 BID, no missed doses he can think of.

NKDA. Never smoker, no alcohol.
ROS: negative. No tremor, no thirst or urinary change.

Exam: vitals as charted. Neck without goiter. Heart regular, no murmur. Lungs clear throughout. Abdomen soft, nontender. Extremities fine. Fine motor normal.
PHQ-9 4, mostly sleep and energy items; he links it to exam prep.

A/P
1. Bipolar I on lithium: annual BMP, TSH, CBC and lithium level drawn; results to psychiatry.
2. Sleep: talked about keeping a regular schedule through exam season, which his psychiatrist has also stressed with him.
3. Flu and updated COVID given.
Next physical in a year.

documents.title: Results
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Gavin, your labs are back and look good. Sodium, kidney function, calcium, thyroid and blood counts are normal and the lithium level is 0.7. Forwarded to psychiatry. Good luck with quals.

Called pt: he has 4 days left and his psychiatrist is away this week. Called the psychiatry office, the covering psychiatrist will send it today. Pharmacy updated, pt aware. No Rx sent from here.

documents.title: Always thirsty
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, this has been going on since the end of October and I kept thinking it would stop. I'm thirsty constantly and peeing all the time, including getting up two or three times a night. I carry a big water bottle everywhere now and refill it maybe 5 times a day. No other symptoms really. Is this something with the lithium? Can I come in this week?

documents.title: RE: Always thirsty
documents.author: RN
documents.body: Good morning Gavin. Yes, we'd like to see you. You're booked Thursday 1/30 at 9:00. Please come fasting (water is fine, keep drinking as much as you need) so we can check sugar along with the other labs. Keep taking your lithium as prescribed. If you get confused, very weak or start vomiting before then, go to the emergency department.

events.reason: Increased thirst and urination for 3 months

procedures.procedure: Office visit, established patient, moderate MDM

documents.title: Office Visit
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
CC: thirst and frequent urination, about 3 months.

HPI: 26 y/o with bipolar I disorder on lithium for years. Since roughly the end of October he has been thirsty all day and urinating large volumes, up 2-3 times a night. Estimates he drinks well over 4 liters a day, mostly water, no soda or juice. Not losing weight, appetite normal, no blurred vision. No headache, no new meds or supplements, no change in lithium dose. Mood stable, last psychiatry visit in December.

PMH: bipolar I disorder. PSH: tonsillectomy age 8.
Meds: lithium carbonate 600 mg BID (psychiatry). Nothing else.
Allergies: NKDA.
FHx: mother with bipolar disorder and autoimmune thyroiditis, father with hypertension.
Social: grad student, never smoker, no alcohol.

Exam: vitals all within normal limits, weight about where it was in September. Looks well, mucous membranes moist. Thyroid normal. Heart and lungs normal. Abdomen soft, no bladder distension. No edema. No tremor. Neuro intact.

A/P
Polyuria and polydipsia in a long-term lithium user. Lithium-related concentrating defect is at the top of the list; need to exclude diabetes mellitus and look at sodium and calcium. Fasting today.
- BMP, urinalysis, fasting glucose, lithium level now.
- Keep drinking to thirst, do not restrict fluids.
- Will call him with results this afternoon.
- Not changing lithium on my own; will loop in his psychiatrist depending on results.

documents.title: Result Note
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
Labs back from this morning: sodium 148 (high), urine specific gravity 1.001, fasting glucose 97, urine glucose negative, calcium and creatinine normal, lithium 0.8.

Very dilute urine with a high-normal-to-high sodium while drinking freely, and no diabetes. Fits lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. Added to problem list.

Called pt and went over it. Plan:
- Nephrology referral placed for confirmation and management advice.
- Keep water with him at all times, never let himself get behind on fluids, especially in heat, exercise or with any vomiting illness.
- Lithium unchanged for now. I'll write to his psychiatrist today about whether to continue.
- He knows to go to the ED for confusion, vomiting or inability to keep up with fluids.
He was relieved it isn't diabetes.

documents.title: Letter to outpatient psychiatry
documents.author: PCP
documents.body:
To his outpatient psychiatrist, re: Gavin Michaud, DOB 04/30/1998

I saw Gavin yesterday for 3 months of polyuria and polydipsia. Sodium 148, urine specific gravity 1.001, fasting glucose 97, creatinine and calcium normal, lithium level 0.8. I think he has lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus and have referred him to nephrology to confirm.

He has done well on lithium for years and I know that weighs heavily. I would value your view on whether to continue lithium, and will forward the nephrology recommendations when we have them. Labs attached.

Primary care physician

documents.title: Psychiatry reply letter
documents.author: psychiatry
documents.body:
Outpatient Psychiatry
Re: Gavin Michaud

Thank you for your letter and the labs. I saw Mr. Michaud on 02/10. He has been euthymic on lithium for years, and coming off it is not something he wants to try while finishing his dissertation. We discussed the renal finding together. Our shared decision is to continue lithium carbonate 600 mg twice daily without change for now and to revisit after nephrology weighs in. He understands the importance of hydration.

Current medications: lithium carbonate 300 mg capsules, 2 caps PO BID.
Allergies: none known.

Attending psychiatrist

documents.title: Nephrology consultation
documents.author: nephrology
documents.body:
[Received 06/11/2025 following our office's request; visit date 03/12/2025]

OUTPATIENT NEPHROLOGY CONSULTATION
Referring: primary care physician
Reason: polyuria and polydipsia on lithium

History: 26-year-old man with bipolar I disorder, on lithium carbonate since 2016, currently 600 mg twice daily, with about four to five months of thirst and high urine output, drinking 4 to 5 liters a day and waking at night to void. Primary care labs in January showed sodium 148 and urine specific gravity 1.001 with a normal fasting glucose.

Medications: lithium carbonate 600 mg PO BID. Allergies: NKDA.

Exam: BP and pulse normal. Euvolemic. Heart and lungs unremarkable. No edema.

Data (this visit): sodium 146 mEq/L, creatinine 0.86 mg/dL, serum osmolality 302 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 104 mOsm/kg at baseline. Desmopressin 2 mcg given subcutaneously in clinic; urine osmolality at 2 hours 116 mOsm/kg.

Impression: The urine stays maximally dilute despite a high-normal serum osmolality and barely moves after desmopressin. This confirms nephrogenic diabetes insipidus, which in his case is attributable to lithium. Filtration is preserved.

Recommendations:
1. Unrestricted access to water at all times; avoid situations where he cannot drink.
2. Lithium may continue in agreement with his psychiatrist, who has discussed it with him.
3. We talked about amiloride. He finds the symptoms manageable and prefers to wait; reasonable to defer and revisit if they worsen.
4. Sodium and creatinine with his routine labs.
5. Follow-up with us as needed.

Outpatient nephrology

documents.title: Emergency department record
documents.author: emergency medicine
documents.body:
[Received 08/20/2026 with the inpatient records; date of service 07/29/2026]

EMERGENCY DEPARTMENT PHYSICIAN NOTE
Arrival 11:40 by private car with roommate.

HPI: 28-year-old man with bipolar I disorder and lithium-related nephrogenic DI, brought in by his roommate, who found him confused and sleepy this morning after several days of increasing tiredness. He vomited multiple times overnight and today. Roommate noticed his speech was slurred for a while this morning. Patient was discharged from an inpatient psychiatric unit roughly two weeks ago after a manic episode and was started there on a new mood stabilizer, which per the bottles brought in is divalproex ER 500 mg, two tablets daily, along with his longstanding lithium. Denies alcohol and drugs; roommate agrees. History limited by mental status.

Meds (bottles): lithium carbonate 300 mg caps, 2 BID; divalproex sodium ER 500 mg, 2 tabs daily.
Allergies: NKDA.
PMH: bipolar I disorder; nephrogenic diabetes insipidus. PSH: tonsillectomy.
FHx: mother bipolar disorder, father hypertension.

Triage vitals: T 37.4 C (99.3 F), BP 112/76, HR 92, RR 14.

Exam: drowsy, rouses to voice, oriented to self and place only. Mild scleral icterus. Lungs clear, heart regular. Abdomen soft, nontender, no distension. Asterixis present. No focal weakness, face symmetric, no meningismus.

Results: AST 388, ALT 421, total bilirubin 3.4, ammonia 98 (ref 15-45), PT 23.8 / INR 2.1. Lithium 0.9 (therapeutic). Valproic acid 88. Acetaminophen undetectable. BMP and CBC unremarkable. CT head negative.

MDM: Acute hepatocellular injury with coagulopathy and encephalopathy two weeks after starting valproate, with hyperammonemia. Lithium level not toxic. Leading diagnosis valproate-induced liver injury (toxic liver disease) with hyperammonemic encephalopathy. Divalproex held. IV fluids, antiemetic. Discussed with hospitalist and on-call hepatology; first levocarnitine dose ordered here.

Disposition: admitted to medicine, stable.

Emergency medicine attending

reports.text: Complete abdominal ultrasound with duplex evaluation of the hepatic vasculature. Liver normal in size with homogeneous echotexture and smooth contour; no focal lesion. Main portal vein patent with normal hepatopetal flow. Hepatic veins patent. Gallbladder normal without stones or wall thickening. Common bile duct 3 mm. No intrahepatic ductal dilatation. Spleen and both kidneys normal in size. Pancreas partly obscured by bowel gas, visualized portions normal. No ascites.
reports.conclusion: Normal abdominal ultrasound. Patent hepatic vasculature.

documents.title: Hospital discharge summary
documents.author: hospital medicine
documents.body:
[Received 08/20/2026 after records request of 08/11/2026]

DISCHARGE SUMMARY - Hospital Medicine
Admitted 07/29/2026 from the ED. Discharged 08/03/2026 to home.

Principal diagnosis: Valproate-induced liver injury with hyperammonemic encephalopathy (toxic liver disease).
Other: Bipolar I disorder. Lithium-associated nephrogenic diabetes insipidus.

Hospital course: Admitted two weeks after divalproex ER 1000 mg daily was added during a psychiatric admission for mania, with confusion, asterixis, jaundice, transaminases near 400, ammonia 98 and INR 2.1. Divalproex was discontinued on arrival. Treated with IV levocarnitine and lactulose. Hepatology consulted; viral hepatitis panel (HAV IgM, HBsAg, HBc IgM, HCV antibody) negative; abdominal ultrasound with duplex normal. Lithium was held for the first 24 hours given his mental status, then resumed at his home dose on the recommendation of consult-liaison psychiatry once he was alert; level on arrival was 0.9. Free water was given to match his DI-related losses. Mentation was back to baseline by hospital day 2 and asterixis resolved. Transaminases, bilirubin and INR improved daily.

Discharge labs 08/03: ammonia 36, AST 104, ALT 168, total bilirubin 1.5, PT 15.1 / INR 1.3.

Adverse drug reaction: valproate (divalproex) - liver injury with hyperammonemia. Do not rechallenge. Added to allergy list here.

Discharge medications:
- Lithium carbonate 300 mg caps, 2 caps PO BID (continued)
- STOPPED: divalproex sodium ER 1000 mg daily

Mood: psychiatry recommends lithium alone for now; no manic symptoms during this stay.

Follow-up:
- PCP within 1-2 weeks with hepatic panel and PT/INR.
- Outpatient psychiatry within 1 week (patient to call his psychiatrist).
- Avoid valproate and alcohol; keep water available at all times.

Condition at discharge: alert, oriented, eating, ambulating independently.

Hospitalist attending

documents.title: I was in the hospital
documents.author: patient
documents.body: Hi, wanted to let you know I've had a rough month. I was in a psych unit in July for a manic episode and they added Depakote. About two weeks later I got really sick, confused and throwing up, and my roommate took me to the ER. They said the Depakote hurt my liver and my ammonia was high. I was admitted for 5 days and I'm off it now, just on lithium again. I feel mostly back to normal, just tired. The discharge papers said to see my primary doctor and get liver tests. What should I do?

documents.title: RE: I was in the hospital
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Gavin, I'm sorry, that sounds like a frightening few weeks, and I'm glad you're feeling better. Yes, I'd like to see you in the next week and repeat your liver tests and clotting test. Please call the office or reply here and the front desk will get you in, and we can draw labs the same day. We'll request the hospital records. In the meantime no alcohol and no Tylenol beyond the occasional dose, keep up the water, and keep your follow-up with your psychiatrist. If you get yellow, confused, very sleepy or can't keep fluids down, go back to the ED.

documents.title: Records request - hospital
documents.author: MA
documents.body: Per PCP, records requested from the hospital: ED record 7/29 and inpatient stay 7/29-8/3 including discharge summary, labs and imaging. Pt also reports a psychiatric unit stay in early-mid July; he isn't sure of the unit's fax and will send the name. Request faxed to hospital HIM.

documents.title: Outside records review
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Reviewed ED record and discharge summary received yesterday. Valproate liver injury with hyperammonemic encephalopathy, admitted 7/29-8/3; divalproex stopped; lithium resumed at 600 BID. Discharge AST 104, ALT 168, bili 1.5, INR 1.3, ammonia 36. Viral serologies negative, ultrasound normal. Repeat hepatic panel and INR were due 1-2 weeks after discharge and have not been done. He has not booked yet. Psych unit summary not received; he never sent the unit's name. Will reach out again.

documents.title: Checking in
documents.author: PCP
documents.body: Hi Gavin, I got your hospital records and read through them. Your liver numbers were heading the right way when you left, and now we need to check that they finished getting better. Please book a visit this week or next. Also, if you can send me the name of the psychiatric unit from July, we'll ask for those records too.

documents.title: Outreach call
documents.author: front desk
documents.body: Called per PCP to schedule post-hospital visit with labs. Voicemail; left callback number and mentioned next week's openings. Portal message from 8/21 shows as read, no reply yet. Nothing booked.
